title: Git Hooks: From pre-commit to pre-push
summary: A dense study-notes carousel covering how Git hooks work internally, the everyday client-side hooks (pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push), the client-vs-server split, and the modern tooling ecosystem (commitlint, lint-staged, husky) for enforcing quality at commit time.

chapters.title: What Are Git Hooks?
points: Definition: hooks are executable scripts Git runs automatically at fixed lifecycle points (before/after commit, push, merge, rebase).
Location: stored in .git/hooks/; every repo gets sample files (*.sample) on git init — rename them (drop .sample) to activate.
No extension requirement: hooks can be bash, Python, Node, Perl — anything executable; Git just runs them and reads the exit code.
Contract: exit 0 = proceed; non-zero = abort the operation; error text printed to stdout goes to the user's terminal.
Hooks are NOT versioned: .git/ is never committed, so a fresh clone starts with zero active hooks — the core sharing problem (later chapters).
Naming is fixed by Git: you cannot invent new hook names; only the documented set fires.
Two families: client-side (run on YOUR machine, per-operation) vs server-side (run on the remote, on receive).
Use cases: lint, format, run tests, validate commit messages, reject large files, block merges to protected branches.
Quick demo: a minimal pre-commit script with #!/bin/sh and 'exit 1' shows Git aborting every commit.
Callout: hooks only fire on Git CLI operations run in that repo — GUI clients and git wrapper tools usually honor them, but bare scripts bypassing git may not.
git init template dir: hooks can be seeded via `git config init.templateDir` or system templates — one sharing mechanism.
Summary line: hooks = local quality gates with zero dependencies, but weak guarantees because they are opt-out.

layout.note: hooks are not versioned — the sharing gotcha

chapters.title: Hook Mechanics & Internals
points: core.hooksPath config: overrides .git/hooks globally or per-repo — the basis of husky and most sharing tools (`git config core.hooksPath .githooks`).
Execution detail: Git runs hooks with the repo root as cwd (for most hooks), no arguments unless the hook type supplies them.
stdin matters: some hooks receive input — commit-msg gets the message file path as $1; pre-push gets remote name + URL, then ref lines on stdin.
Environment: hooks inherit your shell environment plus GIT_DIR etc.; PATH differences can make a hook work on your machine and fail in CI.
Shebang discipline: #!/bin/sh vs #!/usr/bin/env bash — portability depends on it; missing shebang silently fails on some systems.
Aborting behavior per hook: pre-commit aborts before the commit object exists; commit-msg aborts after object creation but before the ref moves.
Hook failure output: stderr/stdout shown to user — print a helpful message and exit 1, don't fail silently.
Skipping hooks: `git commit --no-verify` (or -n) bypasses pre-commit AND commit-msg — anyone can skip them, so hooks are advisory, not enforcement.
Server-side hooks are the real enforcement layer because the client cannot bypass them.
Performance rule: keep hooks fast (<a few seconds); slow pre-commit hooks train developers to use --no-verify.
Debug technique: run the hook manually (.git/hooks/pre-commit) or `sh -x` it to see exactly what fails.
Diagram: timeline — `git commit` → pre-commit → (snapshot) → commit-msg → commit created → post-commit; abort points marked.

chapters.title: pre-commit Hook: Gating the Commit
points: Fires before the commit message editor and before the commit object is created — the earliest client gate.
No arguments passed; inspect the staged changes yourself with `git diff --cached --name-only`.
Classic pattern: run the linter only on staged files — fast and focused (`git diff --cached --name-only | grep '\.js$' | xargs eslint`).
Gotcha: if your hook auto-fixes files (prettier --write), the fixes are NOT staged — must `git add` them back inside the hook, or commit proceeds with unfixed content.
That auto-fix/staging mismatch is exactly the problem lint-staged solves (later chapter).
A failed pre-commit aborts, but your working tree changes are untouched — safe to fix and re-commit.
Common uses: eslint/stylelint, format check, block debugger/console.log, secret scanning (gitleaks), run fast unit tests.
Do NOT run slow integration suites in pre-commit — that belongs in pre-push or CI.
Race with partial staging: developer stages only some hunks; `git stash --keep-index` inside the hook lets you test exactly the staged snapshot.
Example skeleton: check for TODO in staged files, echo error, exit 1.
Pre-commit framework (Python tool): .pre-commit-config.yaml declares per-file hook sets, manages venvs, `pre-commit run --all-files`.
Rule of thumb: pre-commit = seconds, deterministic, fix-forward errors only.

layout.note: auto-fix isn't staged — lint-staged exists for this
keep it under a few seconds or users skip it

chapters.title: commit-msg Hook: Enforcing Message Standards
points: Fires after pre-commit with one argument: path to a temp file containing the proposed message ($1).
Validate by reading that file; exit non-zero to reject the commit with your error message.
Conventional Commits standard: `type(scope): description` — e.g. feat(auth): add OAuth login; enables semantic versioning and changelog automation.
commitlint: `npm i -D @commitlint/cli @commitlint/config-conventional` + commitlint.config.js `{ extends: ['@commitlint/config-conventional'] }`.
Wire it up with a one-line commit-msg hook: `npx --no-install commitlint --edit $1`.
Useful rules: type-enum (whitelist types), subject-case, subject-empty, header-max-length (usually 72–100 chars).
Local test without committing: `echo 'foo' | commitlint` prints which rule failed — great for debugging config.
Gotcha: squash-merges and merge commits can bypass your rules; configure types like 'Merge' or relax rules for merge commits.
Template alternative: `git commit --template` / commit.template gives a skeleton but doesn't enforce — hook enforcement is the point.
Benefits cascade: commitlint + standard-version/release-please generate CHANGELOGs and version bumps from history automatically.
post-commit fires after the ref moves — too late to reject; only useful for notifications or metrics.
prepare-commit-msg runs BEFORE the editor: use it to inject issue numbers or squash hints into the default message.

chapters.title: pre-push Hook: The Last Client Line
points: Fires after `git push` creates local objects but BEFORE the remote accepts anything — the last client-side chance to stop.
Arguments: $1 = remote name, $2 = remote URL; stdin receives lines like `local_ref local_sha remote_ref remote_sha`.
Because it runs before transfer, a failing pre-push saves bandwidth AND rejects the whole push.
Classic use: run the full test suite before pushing (`npm test`), so broken code never reaches CI or teammates.
Gotcha: deleting a branch sends remote_sha of all zeros (0000...) — handle it or your `git show $sha` calls crash.
New branches also have zero remote_sha; local_sha may be all zeros on deletes — always guard for zero SHAs.
Read stdin in a loop: `while read local_ref local_sha remote_ref remote_sha; do ... done` — never assume one branch.
Trade-off: full test suite can take minutes → developers run `git push --no-verify` under deadline pressure; keep pre-push focused on integration-critical checks.
Diff range trick: `git diff --stat $remote_sha..$local_sha` shows exactly what this push delivers, for targeted checks.
Also used for: pre-push lint of all commits (`git log --format=%s remote_sha..local_sha` piped to commitlint), large-file detection.
pre-receive (server) can do the same checks but pre-push fails faster and keeps the developer in flow.
Rule: pre-commit = fast/local, pre-push = slower/integration, CI = authoritative.

chapters.title: Server-Side Hooks: Real Enforcement
points: Server hooks live in the bare repo's hooks/ dir on the remote (e.g. /srv/git/project.git/hooks/) and run on push events.
The three: pre-receive (once per push, all refs, aborts everything on exit≠0), update (per-ref, per-ref decision), post-receive (after refs move — notifications).
pre-receive reads ref updates from stdin: `old_sha new_sha refname` per line — one rejection rejects the WHOLE push.
update hook takes three args ($1 old, $2 new, $3 refname) — reject one branch while allowing others; preferred for per-branch policies.
Real enforcement: clients cannot --no-verify past server hooks — this is where branch protection actually happens.
Policies to implement: forbid pushes to main, reject non-ff pushes, block large files (`find . -size +100M` on new objects), required commit-message checks.
Zero-SHA again: new_sha = 0000... means delete; old_sha = 0000... means new branch — branch-deletion protection hooks rely on this.
Requires server access: on GitHub.com you cannot install arbitrary hooks — use the API/branch protection or GitHub Apps instead.
Self-hosted GitLab/Gitea/Gitolite support server hooks; GitLab calls them 'push rules' in paid tiers plus custom hooks dirs.
post-receive patterns: deploy triggers, chat notifications, CI kick-off — must never exit non-zero to reject (too late anyway).
Keep server hooks fast and crash-proof: a hanging pre-receive blocks ALL pushes to that repo for everyone.
Split of trust: client hooks = convenience/feedback, server hooks = policy/enforcement.

layout.note: GitHub.com: no raw server hooks — use apps/API
client hooks advise; server hooks enforce

chapters.title: Client vs Server: Comparison & Threat Model
points: Trigger point: client hooks run before the operation completes locally; server hooks run during receive-pack on the remote.
Bypass: client hooks avoidable via --no-verify or by simply never installing them; server hooks unavoidable for push traffic.
Audience: client hooks protect the individual developer (fast feedback in flow); server hooks protect the team (guaranteed policy).
Latency tolerance: client hooks must be < seconds; server hooks get a bit more budget but still block everyone while running.
Environment determinism: client hooks run on unpredictable dev machines; server hooks run in one controlled environment — easier to keep dependencies working.
Mistake pattern: putting critical checks ONLY in pre-commit = zero actual enforcement; duplicate the check in CI + server.
Defense-in-depth stack: pre-commit (instant) → pre-push (thorough) → server hook (policy) → CI (authoritative, async).
CI is not a hook but serves the same role async: it can run minutes-long suites and reverts via revert-merge, not rejection.
post-* hooks can't veto: post-commit, post-receive, post-merge fire after the fact — only observe, never enforce.
Table of all major hooks: pre-commit / prepare-commit-msg / commit-msg / pre-rebase / pre-push | pre-receive / update / post-receive, with timing and veto power.
pre-rebase gotcha: default samples guard against rebasing already-pushed commits — rewriting shared history is the risk it flags.
Rule: pick the latest (closest to truth) and cheapest hook that catches the error class you care about.

chapters.title: Sharing Hooks Across a Team
points: The problem restated: .git/hooks is untracked, so `git clone` delivers zero hooks — every teammate would hand-install.
Option 1 — commit hooks in a tracked dir (.githooks/) + `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`; simple, but each dev must run the config command once.
Option 2 — husky: npm package that sets core.hooksPath to .husky/ and is auto-configured by an `npm install` lifecycle script; de facto JS standard.
husky v8 usage: `npx husky init`, then add commands like `npx lint-staged` to .husky/pre-commit; supports all client hook types.
Option 3 — pre-commit framework (Python): committed YAML config, auto-installs hook environments on first run; language-agnostic hooks.
Option 4 — git template dir: `git config init.templateDir` seeds hooks on every future clone/init (not retroactive for existing clones).
Bootstrap script pattern: a setup.sh that runs `git config core.hooksPath` — commit it and document in README.
Versioning win: when hooks live in the repo, hook changes ship through code review like any other change.
Gotcha: core.hooksPath is relative to the repo root when set locally, but must be absolute-ish in some tool setups — test after cloning.
Security: hooks in a tracked repo execute arbitrary code on contributors' machines — review hook changes with the same rigor as CI config.
Monorepo/multi-language: prefer pre-commit framework or plain core.hooksPath over husky if not a Node project.
Verify step: `git config core.hooksPath` should print your dir; if it prints nothing, hooks in .githooks/ are dead.

chapters.title: commitlint + lint-staged Patterns
points: lint-staged concept: run linters/formatters ONLY on staged files — full-repo linting on every commit wastes time and flags others' WIP.
Setup: `npm i -D lint-staged husky`, then wire .husky/pre-commit to `npx lint-staged`.
Config (package.json or lint-staged.config.js): `"*.{js,ts}": ["eslint --fix", "prettier --write"]` — glob → command list.
lint-staged auto-re-stages fixes: it adds the modified files back before the commit proceeds — solves the pre-commit auto-fix gotcha.
Command rules: each command must exit 0 on success; if any fail, lint-staged aborts the commit and restores state via automatic backup.
Chaining pattern: `"*.{css,scss}": ["stylelint --fix"]`, `"*.{json,md}": ["prettier --write"]`, `"*.py": ["black", "flake8"]`.
Use `--no-error-on-unmatched-pattern` for sparse repos; use `--relative` for tools that need paths relative to cwd.
Full stack recipe: husky → pre-commit runs lint-staged → commit-msg runs commitlint → pre-push runs tests; all configured in one npm install.
commitlint config deep-dive: rules array format `[level, applied, value]` e.g. `['error', 'type-enum', ['feat','fix','chore','docs']]`.
Scope enforcement for monorepos: `scope-enum` rule listing package names keeps history filterable per workspace.
Common mistakes: forgetting to install peer config packages; commitlint.config.js in wrong dir; hooks silently inert because core.hooksPath still points at .husky from an old install.
CI double-check: run `commitlint --from origin/main --to HEAD` in CI so merges/squashes that bypassed local hooks still get validated.

chapters.title: Pitfalls, Trade-offs & Closing Summary
points: Mistake 1: slow hooks (30s+ test suites in pre-commit) → team-wide --no-verify habit → zero enforcement. Budget: seconds for pre-commit, minutes for CI.
Mistake 2: auto-fixing without re-staging → commit contains the broken version even though the hook 'ran prettier'. Fix: lint-staged or `git add -u` in hook.
Mistake 3: hooks not installed on teammates' clones because core.hooksPath was never configured — always add a bootstrap step to onboarding docs.
Mistake 4: relying on client hooks for critical policy — one --no-verify defeats them; mirror the check server-side or in CI.
Mistake 5: hooks breaking on other environments — hardcode bash paths, assume macOS-only tools; test on Linux, use /usr/bin/env, pin tool versions.
Mistake 6: non-zero-SHA crashes in pre-push/pre-receive on branch create/delete — always check for 0000... SHAs.
Mistake 7: rejecting with no message — always print WHY the hook failed and HOW to fix it; silent exit 1 wastes everyone's time.
Trade-off table: friction vs safety, instant feedback vs CI authority, per-file speed vs full-repo certainty.
When to skip hooks entirely: throwaway repos, solo experiments, or when CI+branch protection already covers the risk cheaply.
Evolution path: hand-written sh hooks → husky/lint-staged (Node) or pre-commit framework (polyglot) → server rules as the team grows.

Closing summary: hooks are Git's extension points at every lifecycle moment; pre-commit guards content, commit-msg guards history quality, pre-push guards the remote boundary, server hooks enforce for real.
Final checklist: hooks versioned & bootstrapped ✓ fast ✓ good error messages ✓ duplicated in CI ✓ server-side policy for the rules that truly matter.
